lessons.title: Grinding, Mixing, and Conditioning
lessons.body: Grinding is the first step in feed processing. You need to reduce ingredients to the right particle size so fish can digest them. For most farm-made feeds, a hammer mill is used. A screen size of 1-2 mm is good for tilapia and catfish. If you grind too fine (like powder), pellets may turn to mush in water. If too coarse, ingredients separate and fish cannot eat them. In Africa, many small-scale farmers use locally made hammer mills powered by diesel engines. Always check that your mill is clean and the screen is not worn out. After grinding, mix all ingredients thoroughly. A horizontal mixer or a concrete mixer can be used. For small batches, mix by hand on a clean tarpaulin. Mix for at least 10-15 minutes until you see no streaks of different colors. Conditioning means adding steam or water to the mixed feed before pelleting. This helps starch gelatinize and binds the feed. You can use a simple steam generator or add hot water (about 60-80Â°C) while mixing. The moisture should be around 18-22%. If you add too much water, pellets become sticky and clog the machine. If too little, pellets are dry and crumbly. In many African countries, farmers condition feed by adding cassava starch or gelatinized starch as a binder. A good mix: 100 kg of ground ingredients, 5 kg of cassava starch, and 20 liters of hot water. Mix well until dough-like. Then proceed to pelleting immediately. Remember, grinding, mixing, and conditioning determine the quality of your final pellets. Poor conditioning means poor pellets, which means poor fish growth.

lessons.title: Pelleting and Extrusion Technologies
lessons.body: Pelleting turns your mixed feed into compact pellets that fish can eat easily. There are two main methods: pelleting and extrusion. Pelleting uses a pellet mill that presses the feed through a die. The die has holes of the desired diameter, usually 2-4 mm for fingerlings and 4-6 mm for adult fish. The mill can be powered by a diesel engine or electric motor. In Africa, many small-scale farmers use locally fabricated pellet mills. The feed is fed into the mill, and the rollers push it through the die. The pellets come out hot and soft; they harden as they cool. Extrusion is different: it uses high temperature and pressure to cook the feed, then pushes it through a die. Extrusion makes floating pellets, which are good for tilapia and catfish because you can see if they are eating. Pelleting usually makes sinking pellets. For small-scale farmers, extrusion may be too expensive, but you can buy a small extruder (capacity 50-100 kg/hour) for around $500-$1000. If you cannot afford an extruder, you can make floating pellets by adding a floating agent like expanded clay or by using a steam conditioner and a pellet mill with a special die. The key is to adjust the moisture and temperature. For pelleting, the feed should have 15-20% moisture and be heated to 70-80Â°C. For extrusion, moisture is 20-25% and temperature is 120-150Â°C. After pelleting or extrusion, the pellets must be dried and cooled. Never bag hot pellets; they will mold. Let them cool on a clean surface for 30-60 minutes. Test pellet durability: take a handful, shake them in a bucket of water for 5 minutes. If they hold shape, good. If they disintegrate, adjust your binder or moisture. Always keep records of your settings so you can repeat good batches.

lessons.title: Drying and Cooling of Pellets
lessons.body: After pelleting or extrusion, pellets are hot and wet. If you bag them immediately, they will sweat, grow mold, and become toxic. Drying and cooling are critical steps to reduce moisture to a safe level (10-12%) and bring pellets to room temperature. In Africa, most small-scale farmers use sun drying. Spread pellets in a thin layer (2-3 cm) on a clean concrete floor, tarpaulin, or wire mesh. Turn them every 30 minutes. On a sunny day (30-35Â°C), pellets dry in 4-6 hours. If it is cloudy or humid, drying may take 1-2 days. Never dry on bare ground; dirt and moisture will contaminate the feed. For larger operations, use a mechanical dryer. A simple rotary dryer or a cabinet dryer can be built locally. A cabinet dryer uses a fan and a heat source (electric or charcoal). Set temperature at 50-60Â°C. Higher temperatures can cook the pellets and destroy vitamins. Dry until moisture is 10-12%. You can test moisture by weighing a sample before and after drying, or use a moisture meter (costs about $50). Cooling is done after drying. Spread pellets in a shaded, well-ventilated area. A fan can speed cooling. Pellets should be at room temperature before bagging. If you bag warm pellets, condensation forms inside the bag, leading to mold. A good rule: if you can hold a pellet in your hand for 10 seconds without feeling heat, it is cool enough. In humid regions like coastal West Africa, drying can be challenging. Use a solar dryer or a combination of sun and fan. Always store dried pellets in clean, dry sacks (polypropylene or jute) and keep them off the floor on pallets. Proper drying and cooling prevent aflatoxin and extend shelf life.

lessons.title: Coating and Top-Dressing with Oils and Additives
lessons.body: Coating and top-dressing are ways to add oils, vitamins, minerals, or medicines to finished pellets. This is important because some nutrients, especially oils and vitamins, are destroyed by heat during pelleting or extrusion. So you add them after drying and cooling. The most common coating is with fish oil or vegetable oil. Oils are energy sources and make pellets more palatable. Use 2-5% oil by weight. For example, for 10 kg of pellets, use 200-500 ml of oil. Put pellets in a mixer or a large basin. Slowly pour oil while mixing. Mix for 5-10 minutes until all pellets are shiny. Do not add too much oil; it can cause pellets to clump and clog feeders. You can also top-dress with vitamin premix. Use a premix that contains vitamins A, D, E, and K. Follow the manufacturer's instructions, usually 0.5-1% of feed weight. Mix well. For medication, like antibiotics, only use if prescribed by a vet. Add according to dosage. In Africa, some farmers use local oils like palm oil or groundnut oil. These are good but can go rancid if stored too long. Always use fresh oil. Another additive is a binder like gelatinized starch or guar gum. You can spray a thin layer of starch solution on pellets to reduce fines. After coating, let pellets dry in shade for 1-2 hours to absorb oil. Do not sun-dry coated pellets; oil can become rancid. Store coated pellets in airtight containers. Coating improves feed efficiency and fish health. But remember, never coat with oil if you plan to store for more than 2 months; oil oxidizes and becomes toxic. For long storage, use antioxidants like ethoxyquin (follow dosage) or store in cool, dark place.

lessons.title: Quality Control in Feed Manufacturing
lessons.body: Quality control means checking your feed at every step to ensure it is safe and nutritious. Start with ingredients: smell them, look for mold, insects, or lumps. Never use spoiled ingredients. For each batch, record the date, ingredients, and amounts. After grinding, check particle size: it should be uniform. For mixing, take a sample from different parts of the mixer; if colors differ, mix more. After conditioning, check moisture: squeeze a handful; it should hold shape but not drip water. After pelleting, check pellet durability: put 10 pellets in a glass of water. They should not disintegrate within 30 minutes. Also check pellet size: use a ruler. For drying, use a moisture meter or the salt test: mix 10 g of ground feed with 100 ml of water and 10 g of salt; if moisture is high, the mixture is cloudy. For coating, check oil distribution: pellets should be evenly shiny. For final product, send a sample to a lab if possible. In Africa, many countries have agricultural labs that test feed for protein, fat, fiber, and aflatoxin. Aflatoxin is a big risk from moldy maize or groundnut cake. Test with a simple aflatoxin test kit (costs about $20). If positive, discard the batch. Also check for salmonella and E. coli. Good quality control saves money and fish. Keep a logbook of all tests. Train your workers on hygiene: wash hands, wear clean clothes, keep rodents out. A simple quality control plan: (1) inspect ingredients, (2) monitor moisture and temperature, (3) test pellet durability, (4) test for aflatoxin, (5) store properly. If you sell feed, quality control builds trust and repeat customers.

lessons.title: Storage and Shelf-Life of Finished Feeds
lessons.body: Finished feed must be stored properly to keep it fresh. The main enemies are moisture, heat, light, and pests. Store feed in a cool, dry, dark place. Ideal temperature is below 25Â°C and humidity below 60%. In many African countries, this means a well-ventilated store with a concrete floor and a roof that does not leak. Use pallets to keep bags off the floor (at least 10 cm). Stack bags no more than 10 high to avoid crushing. Leave space between stacks and walls for air circulation. Use clean, dry sacks. Polypropylene bags are good, but they are not airtight. For long storage, use airtight containers or silos. If you use bags, tie them tightly. Never store feed near chemicals, fuel, or pesticides. Shelf life depends on the feed type. Uncoated dry pellets can last 2-3 months if stored well. Coated pellets with oil last only 1-2 months because oil goes rancid. Feeds with high fishmeal or meat meal spoil faster. Always use the first-in, first-out rule: sell or use older feed first. Check stored feed every week for mold, insects, or off-smells. If you see mold, discard the whole batch; do not just remove the moldy parts. Insects can be controlled by keeping the store clean and using food-grade diatomaceous earth. For long-term storage, you can add antioxidants like BHT or ethoxyquin (follow instructions). In humid regions, use a dehumidifier or charcoal to absorb moisture. A simple test for freshness: smell the feed. Good feed smells like fish or grains. Bad feed smells sour, musty, or like paint. Also, if pellets are sticky or clumped, moisture has entered. Proper storage saves money and ensures your fish get good nutrition. Never feed moldy feed to fish; it can cause disease and death.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Feed Processing and Manufacturing

This practical reference consolidates the operational knowledge a small-to-medium fish feed manufacturer in Africa needs to turn raw ingredients into saleable, safe, and profitable pellets. It covers the full processing chain â grinding, mixing, conditioning, pelleting, extrusion, drying, cooling, coating, quality control, and storage â with the business lens: every decision should reduce cost, reduce loss, or increase the price your feed can command. Whether you are producing 500 kg/day for your own tilapia ponds or 5 tonnes/day for sale to catfish farmers, the same principles apply.

Fish feed manufacturing in Africa is a margin business. Ingredient costs typically represent 60â75% of total production cost, and processing losses (fines, over-drying, spoilage, rejected batches) can erode another 10â20% if not controlled. The lessons below are ordered as a production line, but the quality control and storage sections apply across all stages.

1. Grinding, Mixing, and Conditioning

Grinding reduces particle size so that ingredients mix uniformly and pellets bind well. For tilapia and catfish, a hammer mill with a 1.5â2.0 mm screen is standard; for fry feed, 0.5â0.8 mm is required. Finer grinding increases surface area, improves digestibility, and produces stronger pellets, but it also increases energy cost and dust. A practical rule: grind maize, soybean meal, and fishmeal to pass a 1 mm screen for floating feed; use 2 mm for sinking feed where water stability is less critical.

Mixing must achieve a coefficient of variation (CV) below 10% for critical ingredients such as vitamins, minerals, and amino acids. Horizontal ribbon mixers or vertical screw mixers are common in African workshops. Mixing time is typically 3â5 minutes for a ribbon mixer; over-mixing can cause segregation of particles of different densities. Always add micro-ingredients after the bulk ingredients are blended, and use a premix carrier (e.g., ground maize or rice bran) to avoid clumping.

Conditioning adds steam (or water in small operations) to raise temperature and moisture before pelleting. Conditioned mash at 80â90Â°C for 30â60 seconds gelatinises starch, activates binders, and lubricates the die. In small African operations without a boiler, hot water (60â80Â°C) can be added in the mixer, but this is less consistent. Conditioned feed should feel like damp sand and form a ball when squeezed, not drip water.

2. Pelleting and Extrusion Technologies

Pelleting compresses conditioned mash through a die to form dense, sinking pellets. It is cheaper than extrusion and suits catfish and tilapia grow-out feeds where water stability of 10â30 minutes is acceptable. A pellet mill with a 3â6 mm die is typical. Key variables: die speed, steam pressure, and moisture. Pellets should be firm, not crumbly, and should not shatter when dropped from 1 metre.

Extrusion uses higher temperature (100â150Â°C), pressure, and shear to gelatinise starch and expand the pellet, producing floating feed. Extrusion is essential for high-value tilapia and ornamental fish feeds, and for feeds containing high levels of plant protein. Single-screw extruders are common in Africa; twin-screw extruders are more flexible but costlier. Floating feed commands a 10â25% price premium over sinking feed in most African markets because it allows farmers to observe feeding and reduce waste.

3. Drying and Cooling of Pellets

Freshly extruded pellets contain 20â30% moisture and must be dried to 8â12% for safe storage. Drying methods in Africa range from sun-drying on racks (cheap but slow and weather-dependent) to horizontal belt dryers and vertical counter-flow dryers. For a business, a belt dryer with controlled temperature (60â90Â°C) and airflow gives consistent results and protects against aflatoxin growth during slow drying.

Cooling follows drying. Pellets must be cooled to within 5Â°C of ambient temperature before bagging; otherwise condensation inside the bag causes mould. A counter-flow cooler or a simple cooling conveyor with ambient air is sufficient. Do not bag hot pellets â this is one of the most common causes of rejected batches in African feed mills.

4. Coating and Top-Dressing with Oils and Additives

Coating applies oil (fish oil, vegetable oil) or liquid additives (vitamins, enzymes, attractants) to the pellet surface after drying and cooling. This improves energy density, palatability, and water stability. A drum coater or a simple cement mixer can be used. Apply 2â6% oil by weight; higher levels make pellets soft and prone to rancidity. Add antioxidants (e.g., ethoxyquin or natural tocopherols) when oil inclusion exceeds 3%.

Top-dressing is common for high-value feeds: a small amount of fishmeal, krill meal, or synthetic attractant is dusted onto oil-coated pellets to boost smell and taste. This is a low-cost way to differentiate your product in the market.

â  SAFETY WARNING:

Feed manufacturing involves dust, heat, and rotating machinery. Always wear a dust mask and ear protection when operating hammer mills and mixers. Never reach into a pellet mill or extruder while it is running â lock out/tag out before maintenance. Steam lines and dryers cause severe burns; use insulated gloves and check valves daily. Aflatoxin-contaminated ingredients must be rejected or treated â never blend contaminated maize into feed, as toxins concentrate in the pellet and poison fish and, ultimately, consumers. Store fuel and oil away from feed ingredients to prevent contamination and fire risk.

5. Quality Control in Feed Manufacturing

Quality control (QC) is what separates a profitable feed business from one that loses customers. Test at three points: incoming ingredients, in-process mash, and finished pellets. Key tests: moisture (oven or moisture meter), crude protein (Kjeldahl or NIR), fat (Soxhlet), water stability (time to disintegration in water), pellet durability index (PDI), and aflatoxin (rapid test kits). For small producers, a simple daily log of moisture, temperature, and pellet appearance catches most problems before they become rejections.

Business impact: a batch rejected for high moisture or low protein is a direct loss of ingredients, energy, and labour. A customer who receives mouldy feed will not return. QC is not a cost â it is insurance on your reputation and your cash flow.

6. Storage and Shelf-Life of Finished Feeds

Finished feed should be stored in a cool, dry, well-ventilated warehouse, off the floor on pallets, away from walls, and away from direct sunlight. Ideal conditions: below 25Â°C, below 65% relative humidity, and 8â12% feed moisture. Under these conditions, pelleted feed can last 3â6 months; extruded floating feed 2â4 months due to higher oil content. In hot, humid African climates, shelf-life may be shorter â 4â8 weeks in coastal or rainy-season conditions.

Use FIFO (first in, first out) stock rotation. Inspect bags weekly for mould, insects, or off-smells. Never store feed with pesticides, fertiliser, or fuel. For commercial sales, print production dates and batch numbers on bags â this builds trust and allows traceability if a problem occurs.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Grind to the right size: 0.8â1.0 mm for floating tilapia feed; 1.5â2.0 mm for sinking catfish feed. Check screen weekly for wear.
  2. Mix micro-ingredients last: Use a premix carrier and mix 3â5 minutes; test CV annually or when changing mixer.
  3. Condition at 80â95Â°C: Add steam or hot water until mash forms a ball but does not drip. Never skip conditioning â it affects pellet durability.
  4. Dry to 8â12% moisture: Use a moisture meter or oven test. Bag only after cooling to ambient temperature.
  5. Apply oil at 2â6%: Add antioxidant if oil exceeds 3%. Coat after cooling, not before drying.
  6. Test every batch: Moisture, protein, water stability, and aflatoxin (rapid kit). Log results daily.
  7. Store on pallets, FIFO: Below 25Â°C, below 65% humidity, away from chemicals and sunlight. Inspect weekly.
  8. Label every bag: Production date, batch number, protein content, and expiry. Traceability builds customer trust and reduces returns.

Further Reading

  • FAO (2012) â Fish Feed Technology: A Manual for the Preparation of Fish Feed â free PDF, covers grinding, mixing, pelleting, and storage.
  • FAO (2020) â The State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture: Sustainability in Action â includes feed value chain and Africa data.
  • AUDA-NEPAD (2021) â Aquaculture Feed Value Chain in Africa â regional guidelines for feed production and quality.
  • WorldFish Center â Feeds and Fertilizers for Small-Scale Aquaculture â practical, Africa-focused feed formulation and processing.
  • African Aquaculture Association â Technical Resources â regional best practices and training materials.

This practical reference is part of the RISE AFRICA Skills course "Fish Feed Formulation," Module 4: Feed Processing and Manufacturing. Use it alongside your production log and local extension officer. For business planning, calculate your cost per kg of feed at each processing stage â grinding, mixing, pelleting, drying, and coating â to identify where you can reduce waste and increase margin.

quiz.q: What is the recommended screen size for grinding feed for tilapia and catfish?
quiz.explanation: A screen size of 1-2 mm produces the right particle size for good digestion and pellet quality.

quiz.q: How long should you mix feed ingredients to ensure uniformity?
quiz.explanation: Mixing for 10-15 minutes ensures no streaks of different colors remain, indicating a uniform mix.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for conditioning feed before pelleting?
quiz.explanation: 18-22% moisture helps starch gelatinize and binds the feed without making it too sticky.

quiz.q: Which binder is commonly used in Africa for conditioning feed?
quiz.explanation: Cassava starch is widely available and effective as a binder in farm-made feeds.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between pelleting and extrusion?
options: A) Pelleting uses steam, extrusion uses water
B) Pelleting makes sinking pellets, extrusion makes floating pellets
C) Pelleting is for large farms, extrusion for small farms
D) Pelleting uses a die, extrusion does not
quiz.explanation: Extrusion cooks feed at high temperature and pressure, producing floating pellets, while pelleting typically makes sinking pellets.

quiz.q: What is the typical die hole diameter for adult fish pellets?
quiz.explanation: 4-6 mm pellets are suitable for adult fish, while smaller sizes are for fingerlings.

quiz.q: What temperature range is used in extrusion?
quiz.explanation: Extrusion uses high temperature (120-150Â°C) to cook the feed and create floating pellets.

quiz.q: How can you test pellet durability?
options: B) Shake in water for 5 minutes
quiz.explanation: Shaking pellets in water for 5 minutes tests if they hold shape; disintegrating means poor durability.

quiz.q: Why should you not bag hot pellets?
options: B) They will burn the bag
quiz.explanation: Hot pellets release moisture, causing condensation inside the bag, which promotes mold growth.

quiz.q: What is the safe moisture level for dried pellets?
quiz.explanation: 10-12% moisture prevents mold and maintains pellet quality during storage.

quiz.q: How long does sun drying typically take on a sunny day?
quiz.explanation: On a sunny day (30-35Â°C), pellets dry in 4-6 hours when spread thin and turned regularly.

quiz.q: What temperature should a cabinet dryer be set to?
quiz.explanation: 50-60Â°C is safe for drying without cooking the pellets or destroying vitamins.

quiz.q: Why is it important to cool pellets before bagging?
options: B) To prevent condensation and mold
quiz.explanation: Cooling prevents condensation inside bags, which leads to mold and spoilage.

quiz.q: What is the recommended oil inclusion rate for coating pellets?
quiz.explanation: 2-5% oil by weight improves palatability and energy without causing clumping.

quiz.q: Why should you not sun-dry oil-coated pellets?
quiz.explanation: Sunlight and heat cause oil to oxidize and become rancid, harming fish health.

quiz.q: Which vitamin premix is commonly top-dressed on pellets?
options: B) Vitamins A, D, E, K
quiz.explanation: A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble vitamins often added after pelleting to avoid heat destruction.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for moisture in mixed feed?
quiz.explanation: The salt test (mixing feed, water, and salt) shows cloudiness if moisture is high.

quiz.q: Which toxin is a major risk from moldy maize or groundnut cake?
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin is produced by molds on maize and groundnut cake and is highly toxic to fish.

quiz.q: What is the first-in, first-out rule?
options: C) Mix old and new feed
D) Store feed in one place
quiz.explanation: Using older feed first prevents spoilage and ensures freshness.

quiz.q: What is the ideal storage temperature for finished feed?
quiz.explanation: Cool temperatures below 25Â°C slow down spoilage and maintain feed quality.

quiz.q: How high should bags be stacked in storage?
quiz.explanation: Stacking no more than 10 high prevents crushing and allows air circulation.

quiz.q: What is a sign of good quality feed?
options: C) Fresh fish or grain smell
quiz.explanation: Good feed smells like fish or grains; bad odors indicate spoilage.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find mold in stored feed?
quiz.explanation: Mold produces toxins that spread; the entire batch must be discarded to avoid poisoning fish.

quiz.q: Which additive can help control insects in stored feed?
quiz.explanation: Food-grade diatomaceous earth is a safe insecticide for stored feed.

quiz.q: What is the shelf life of uncoated dry pellets stored well?
quiz.explanation: Uncoated dry pellets can last 2-3 months if kept cool, dry, and dark.

quiz.q: Why do coated pellets have a shorter shelf life?
quiz.explanation: Oil in coated pellets oxidizes and becomes rancid, limiting shelf life to 1-2 months.

quiz.q: What is a good practice before bagging pellets?
quiz.explanation: Cooling to room temperature prevents condensation and mold inside bags.

quiz.q: Which factor does NOT affect feed storage?
quiz.explanation: Bag color is irrelevant; light, humidity, and temperature are critical factors.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of conditioning in feed processing?
options: B) To add moisture and heat for binding
quiz.explanation: Conditioning adds moisture and heat to gelatinize starch and bind ingredients before pelleting.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to check if pellets are cool enough to bag?
options: A) Touch with finger for 10 seconds
quiz.explanation: If you can hold a pellet for 10 seconds without feeling heat, it is cool enough.
